title: Robert's Rules of Order Revised for Deliberative Assemblies
source: Henry M. Robert, Robert's Rules of Order Revised for Deliberative Assemblies (Scott, Foresman, 1915), section 59 (the secretary) and section 60 (the minutes); Project Gutenberg eBook #75990.

rules.text: The minutes say the kind of meeting: regular, special or adjourned.
The minutes name the body that met.
The minutes give the date, and the place when it varies.
The regular chair and secretary were present, or the minutes name who stood in.
The minutes say whether the previous minutes were approved or their reading was dispensed with.
Every main motion that was not withdrawn is recorded with what became of it.
A motion names its mover, not its seconder.
Points of order and appeals are recorded with whether they were sustained or lost.
The minutes give the time the meeting opened and the time it adjourned.
A counted or ballot vote gives the numbers; a roll-call vote gives the names.
Minutes record what was done, not what was said, with no praise or blame.
An adopted resolution is written out in full.
The secretary signs the minutes, and the president too when they are published.
Minutes that are not habitually approved at the next meeting carry, at their end, the word Approved, the date of approval and the secretary's signature.
